summary: The English of all five verses is faithful to the Hebrew and consistent with Rashi and Ibn Ezra; no English line needs a change. The faults are in the apparatus: the sense 'hundredth' was filled mechanically for every cardinal מֵאָה, בָּנִים was given the sense 'children' against the gloss 'sons', and the gloss of בָּבֶל omits the meaning the text gives the name, as the decisions require. The translator's note on 11:10 claims the chronology with 5:32 and 7:6 accords when on its face it does not (Ibn Ezra refers the difficulty to 10:21). Several commentary summaries misstate their comments (Rashi on 11:9, Ibn Ezra on 11:9 and 11:10, Radak on 11:9), and two accent notes are inaccurate.

patches.reason: decisions.md: the meaning of a name the text explains (בָּבֶל 11:9) goes in the gloss and the grammar notes. The gloss gave the bare name.

patches.value: the text explains the name by בָּלַל 'he confused'. Ibn Ezra and Radak take בָּבֶל as two words, בָּא בַּל 'confusion came', with the aleph of בָּא dropped; Radak: בַּל is a noun from בָּלַל, like קַן from קָנַן
patches.reason: the learner needs the explanation of the name the text and both commentators give; the token had no note.

value: עַל־כֵּן is a stock phrase introducing an explanation of a name or custom: 'therefore'.
קָרָא has no stated subject; the 3rd masculine singular is impersonal, so 'its name was called'. Ibn Ezra and Radak do not change this.
The etiology rests on wordplay: בָּבֶל (Babel) and בָּלַל (confuse). The verb בָּלַל is a Qal perfect, 'he confused'. Ibn Ezra and Radak analyse the name as בָּא בַּל, 'confusion came'.
שְׂפַת כָּל־הָאָרֶץ: 'the lip of all the earth' means the one speech of 11:1, here 'the language of all the earth'.

The etnaḥta on הָאָרֶץ divides the verse in two: the first half gives the name and its reason (כִּי־שָׁם בָּלַל, 'because there he confused'), the second the scattering (וּמִשָּׁם הֱפִיצָם, 'and from there he scattered them'). The fronted adverbs שָׁם and מִשָּׁם make a pair: 'there ... and from there'.
patches.reason: the last note said the verse is two clauses each beginning with a fronted adverb; the first half begins with עַל־כֵּן קָרָא, and שָׁם heads only the כִּי clause inside it. Also adds the commentators' analysis of the name, as decisions.md requires for the grammar notes.

patches.value: Rashi: 'and from there He scattered them' teaches that they have no share in the world to come. He asks which was worse, the generation of the flood or that of the dispersion, who stretched out a hand against the Root (God) to make war on Him; yet the first were swept away and the second were not destroyed. The answer: the flood generation were robbers with strife among them, while these kept love and fellowship, as it says 'one language and one set of words'; so you learn that dissension is hateful (שֶׁשָּׂנְאוּי הַמַּחֲלֹקֶת) and peace is great. This is homily and does not bear on the English.
patches.reason: the summary rendered שֶׁשָּׂנְאוּי הַמַּחֲלֹקֶת as 'the hatred of dissension is great'; it means 'dissension is hateful'. It also left out the premise of the question: the dispersion generation rebelled against God himself and yet survived.

value.summary: Ibn Ezra: בָּבֶל is two words, בָּא בַּל ('confusion came'), with the aleph of בָּא missing; so also בגד (30:11, for בָּא גָד) and בָּמָה (as if בָּא מָה). The English line keeps the name Babel; the derivation is recorded in the gloss and notes and agrees with the text's link to בָּלַל.

patches.reason: the summary did not say what the two words are and vocalised the Gen 30:11 word as בָּגָד, which hides the point (בָּא גָד). The relation 'follows' contradicted its own summary ('does not rest on the compound derivation'); the reading bears on the notes, not the English line, so 'records'.

patches.value: Radak: one would expect the name to be בַּלֵּל, from בָּלַל; instead it is compounded of two words to bring out the sense more fully, בָּא בַּל, 'confusion came' upon them from heaven. בַּל is a noun from the full root בָּלַל, like קַן from קָנַן and חַן from חָנַן. The English follows the connection with בָּלַל given in the text, which Radak's analysis keeps.
patches.reason: the summary set the compound 'rather than a Pi'el from בָּלַל', as if Radak cut the name off from בָּלַל. He says בַּל itself comes from בָּלַל, and he speaks of an expected form בַּלֵּל, not of a Pi'el.
sense 3 of מֵאָה is 'hundredth', an ordinal; מְאַת here is the cardinal 'a hundred'. The entry lists no other sense, so the sense is removed.

patches.value: construct feminine singular; the entry's only listed sense, 'hundredth', does not fit the cardinal, so no sense is given
patches.reason: records the removal of the wrong sense.

value: אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת opens a new section of the book, here the line of Shem down to Abram.

The name שֵׁם is repeated: first as genitive of the heading, then as subject of a new nominal clause. The zaqef qaton on the first שֵׁם closes the heading; the yetiv, a disjunctive accent set before the word, stands on אֵלֶּה and on the second שֵׁם, at the head of each part.
בֶּן־מְאַת שָׁנָה: age is expressed as 'son of N years', with the number in the construct state.
וַיּוֹלֶד is Hifil wayyiqtol of יָלַד: the father is the subject, 'he fathered'. It continues the age clause: when he was a hundred, he fathered.
שְׁנָתַיִם is the dual of שָׁנָה, 'two years'.
patches.reason: the note said 'the yetiv on both' שֵׁם; the first שֵׁם carries zaqef qaton, the yetiv is on אֵלֶּה and the second שֵׁם.

patches.value: Rashi reads שֵׁם בֶּן־מְאַת שָׁנָה as the age at the time Arpachshad was born, which is two years after the flood; the English joins the age to the begetting with 'when'. On the face of 5:32 and 7:6 (Noah 500 when he fathered his sons, 600 at the flood) Shem would be a hundred at the flood, not two years after it. Ibn Ezra refers the explanation of שְׁנָתַיִם to 10:21, 'the brother of Japheth the elder': Japheth was the first-born and Shem was born later. Radak says he explained it at 5:32.
patches.reason: the note said the figures 'accord'. They do not on their face: 500 + 100 = 600, the year of the flood, not two years after it. Both Ibn Ezra and Radak treat this as a difficulty they have resolved elsewhere.

patches.value: Ibn Ezra: the explanation of שְׁנָתַיִם is given at 10:21, 'the brother of Japheth the elder' (Shem was not the first-born). He then reckons the lifespans: Shem lived 500 years after the flood, Arpachshad 438, Shelah 433, Eber 464, while Peleg lived only 239, half his fathers' years, so Peleg may have been named on the day he was gathered (died). He rejects the view that the tower's builders were seventy, matching seventy languages: Caphtorim and Pathrusim are not individuals, Noah and his sons are not counted, and by Seder Olam the builders were thousands and myriads. This does not alter the English.
patches.reason: the summary left out the comment's main point on the lemma: שְׁנָתַיִם is explained by 10:21, Japheth being the elder. That point bears on the note to this verse.
sense 3 of מֵאָה is 'hundredth'; מֵאוֹת here is the cardinal plural 'hundreds'. The entry lists no fitting sense.

patches.value: plural of מֵאָה; 'five hundreds' means five hundred. The entry's only listed sense, 'hundredth', does not fit the cardinal, so no sense is given
patches.reason: records the removal of the wrong sense.
בָּנִים paired with וּבָנוֹת means 'sons', as the gloss says: sense 1 'son', not sense 2 'children'.

value: וַיְחִי־שֵׁם is the wayyiqtol of חָיָה, 'and Shem lived'.

אַחֲרֵי הוֹלִידוֹ is a preposition with an infinitive construct and a suffix whose referent is the subject: 'after his fathering', 'after he fathered'. The phrase runs from the revia on שֵׁם to the zaqef qaton on אַרְפַּכְשָׁד; the pashta on אַחֲרֵי is a lesser divider within it, and the conjunctive munaḥ joins הוֹלִידוֹ to its object.
The number precedes the noun: חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה 'five hundreds of year', with a singular noun after the number, as in the genealogy formula.
The repeated וַיּוֹלֶד בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת closes each entry of the genealogy.
patches.reason: the note said 'the pashta and munaḥ keep the phrase together'; the pashta is a disjunctive accent, so it divides rather than binds.

verdicts.comment: homily on the fate of the dispersion generation; it does not bear on the English.
the derivation בָּא בַּל leaves the name Babel and its link to בָּלַל as the English has them.
the English gives the age at Arpachshad's birth, two years after the flood, as Rashi reads it.
Ibn Ezra takes 'two years' literally and resolves it by 10:21; the English stands. The translator's note is corrected to match.
